PSHE & RSHE
Equipping pupils with the knowledge, skills and values to thrive in life, relationships and society.
At Headstart School, our Personal, Social, Health and Economic Education (PSHE) and Relationships, Sex and Health Education (RSE) curriculum is designed to equip pupils with the knowledge, skills and values they need to thrive in a diverse and ever-changing world. Rooted in inclusivity and tailored to meet individual learning needs, our approach empowers pupils to develop healthy relationships, understand themselves and others, and make informed life choices.
We follow the comprehensive Jigsaw Programme, which provides a structured and progressive framework from primary through to secondary, covering key topics such as identity, mental health, online safety, healthy lifestyles, and respect for self and others. Our RSE curriculum ensures pupils understand personal boundaries, consent, emotional wellbeing and, at the appropriate stages, the physical and emotional aspects of growing up and relationships.
The curriculum is delivered through weekly lessons, assemblies, pastoral support, and cross-curricular opportunities—reinforcing the importance of personal development, equality, and safeguarding. Our aim is for every young person to leave Headstart as a confident, respectful and responsible member of society, prepared for the opportunities and challenges of adult life.
At Headstart School, we are deeply committed to the personal development of every pupil. Our curriculum goes beyond academic learning to foster pupils’ spiritual, moral, social and cultural (SMSC) understanding. Through an inclusive and broad approach, we help pupils grow into reflective, respectful and responsible individuals who are well-prepared for life in modern Britain.
Our SMSC provision is embedded throughout school life—from subject teaching and enrichment opportunities to assemblies and therapeutic support. Pupils explore their identity, values, and place in society, while developing the confidence and empathy needed to engage positively with others from different backgrounds and beliefs.
We actively promote British Values—democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, mutual respect, and tolerance—ensuring pupils understand their rights and responsibilities as citizens. These principles underpin our approach to Citizenship Education, the Prevent Strategy, and safeguarding. We recognise that some pupils may face challenges due to their special educational needs, and we are committed to supporting them sensitively while upholding high expectations for all.
At Headstart, personal development is not an add-on—it is at the heart of everything we do.

Outdoor Learning at Headstart
At Headstart School, our Forest School and Land-Based Provision are integral to our unique educational approach. Set across two beautiful rural sites in East Sussex, our outdoor learning environments offer pupils immediate access to nature, providing rich opportunities for personal growth, skill development, and emotional wellbeing.
The Forest School programme is designed to foster independence, resilience, and a deep connection with the natural world. Through hands-on, experiential learning, pupils engage in activities such as bushcraft, nature exploration, environmental care, and outdoor problem-solving. These experiences help build confidence, empathy, and practical life skills in a calm, therapeutic setting.
Our staff are trained to deliver Forest School sessions that are inclusive and tailored to the individual needs of our learners, many of whom thrive in non-traditional learning environments. The outdoor curriculum complements classroom learning and supports the development of communication, teamwork, and self-regulation.
Forest School at Headstart is more than just outdoor education—it’s a vital part of our holistic approach to helping pupils grow into confident, capable, and compassionate individuals.

British Values
British Values in action – from democracy to mutual respect.
At Headstart School, British Values are woven into daily life. From democracy and the rule of law to individual liberty, mutual respect, and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs, we help pupils understand the principles that shape our society. Through lessons, assemblies, and everyday interactions, our students learn how these values guide their choices, relationships, and responsibilities both in school and in the wider community.
Democracy
Democracy is an important value at our school. Pupils have an opportunity to have their voices heard through our School Council. The elections of members of the School Council are based on pupil votes. This supports pupils to understand how citizens can influence decision-making through the democratic process. Our School Council is able to genuinely effect change within the school.
The Rule of Law
The importance of laws and rules, whether they are those that govern the class, the school or the country, are consistently reinforced throughout regular school days, as well as when dealing with behaviour and through school assemblies. Pupils are taught the value and reasons behind laws, that they govern and protect us, the responsibilities that this involves and the consequences when laws are broken.
Individual Liberty
Pupils are actively encouraged to make choices at our school, knowing that they are in a safe and supportive environment. As a school we provide boundaries for our children to make choices safely, through the provision of a safe environment and planned curriculum. Pupils are encouraged to know, understand and exercise their rights and personal freedoms and are advised how to exercise these safely, for example through our e-Safety teaching and PHSE education.
Mutual Respect
Children learn that their behaviour has an effect on their own rights and those of others. Students are constantly reminded about working positively with others and how working as part of a team can support the development of positive relationships and an understanding of others. We aim to encourage honesty, trust, and meaningful communication with both staff and students at all times and this is reinforced on a lesson by lesson basis.
Tolerance of Those of Different Faiths and Beliefs
This is achieved through enhancing pupils’ understanding of their place in a culturally diverse society; such work is delivered through the PSHEE programme at all key Stages and through weekly themed assemblies held on a Monday morning. We use opportunities such as the Olympics and World Cups to study and learn about life and culture in other countries and this is further reinforced through the daily themes where specific countries around the world form a key focus.

Headstart Residential Care
Providing safe, nurturing homes where young people with autism can grow, thrive, and feel truly supported.
Headstart Residential Care provides therapeutic residential care for children between the ages of 8 – 18, particularly those on the autism spectrum, with complex needs and that have suffered previous trauma. Our model of care is deeply rooted in therapeutic practices, with staff working closely with therapists to ensure consistent, individualized support.
The PACE (Playfulness, Acceptance, Curiosity and Empathy) Model, developed by Dr Dan Hughes, is the foundation of our practice with staff and therapists integrating Positive Behaviour Support (PBS), Protecting Rights in a Caring Environment (PRICE) and a deep understanding of Autism, ADHD and other diagnosis.
Each child receives a bespoke care plan, designed to meet their unique needs in a safe, structured, and supportive setting. Children are supported teams of highly experienced, well-trained carers who are committed to achieving the best outcomes for the children.
Headstart Reisdential Care prides itself on being small and personal, therapeutic home environments. Children in care also have the opportunity to attend Headstart School, ensuring continuity between care and education.
Our Therapeutic Approach
Headstart Residential Care takes a nurturing and therapeutic approach to supporting young people on the Autistic Spectrum, helping them to thrive in a safe and caring environment. Therapy is integrated into every aspect of daily life, with staff guided by our therapists to provide consistent strategies and continuity of care. Using the PBS (Positive Behaviour Support) model, we focus on building self-esteem and encouraging positive behaviours through reinforcement and encouragement.
Our Dedicated Team
We are proud to have a highly trained and experienced staff team who work closely with young people to achieve the best possible outcomes. Our History
From a barn in the Sussex countryside to a thriving community, our story is one of vision, passion, and perseverance.
The Vision
In 1999, Headstart began with a simple dream: to create a school for children who struggled to fit into mainstream education. Drawing on her own experience as a pupil wanting more from the curriculum, and later as a teacher, Nicki envisioned small classes, a nurturing environment, and a curriculum that built confidence while making learning fun. Her goal was clear — a place where every child felt safe, valued, and inspired to learn.
Finding a Home
Headstart’s first home was a rural barn in East Sussex, filled at the time with hay and potatoes. Nicki invested in building four classrooms, computers, and resources, transforming the space into a school. One memory stands out: her father, a drummer, sat at a kit in the middle of the barn and told her, “It will never work.” Sadly, he didn’t live to see the school thrive, but his doubts were proven joyfully wrong.
The First Pupils
The first class was just four pupils, taught by Nicki in a single classroom with a cupboard for an office. The curriculum was tailored to each child, built on listening to their needs. One boy from London, who had never seen green fields, discovered a passion for Shakespeare and told Nicki, “This is like heaven here.” In that moment, she knew the vision was right.
Building for Autism
Nicki’s next step was to create autism-friendly spaces, with plain walls, outdoor access from every room, and a sensory room with interactive learning tools. The success of this unit led to further growth, shaping Headstart into a school that would go on to specialise in autism and complex needs.
Growth & Vocational Learning
As the school grew, Nicki secured the building outright and welcomed new teachers and vocational specialists. Known locally as “the school on a farm in a barn,” pupils studied core subjects alongside practical skills like farming, bricklaying, decorating, and animal care. These hands-on experiences laid the foundation for the vocational courses that remain central to Headstart today.
Becoming Headstart School
Over time, Headstart formalised its structure, registering as a school, building policies, and expanding its curriculum. Therapies were integrated into daily learning, and pupils who had been out of education for years began achieving qualifications in English, Maths, and vocational skills. Though some educators doubted the model, parents and children believed in it — and pupils thrived.
Today and Beyond
From those humble beginnings, Headstart has grown into two thriving sites with over 60 dedicated staff and therapists. While the scale has changed, the heart of the school remains the same: a place of care, community, and opportunity, where every child can flourish both academically and personally.

Autism
Building awareness, acceptance, and the right support for every child.
The National Autistic Society (NAS) tells us that Autism is a lifelong condition which affects how people communicate and interact with the world. There are approximately 700,000 autistic adults and children in the UK.
How common is autism?
Autism is much more common than most people think. There are around 700,000 autistic people in the UK, that’s more than 1 in 100. People from all nationalities and cultural, religious and social backgrounds can be autistic, although it appears to affect more men than women.
How do autistic people see the world?
Some autistic people say the world feels overwhelming and this can cause them considerable anxiety.
In particular, understanding and relating to other people, and taking part in everyday family, school, work and social life, can be harder. Other people appear to know, intuitively, how to communicate and interact with each other, yet can also struggle to build rapport with autistic people. Autistic people may wonder why they are ‘different’ and feel their social differences mean people don’t understand them.
Autistic people often do not ‘look’ disabled. Some parents of autistic children say that other people simply think their child is naughty, while adults find that they are misunderstood. The NAS are educating the public about autism through our Too Much Information campaign.
Diagnosis:
A diagnosis is the formal identification of autism, usually by a multidisciplinary diagnostic team, often including a speech and language therapist, paediatrician, psychiatrist and/or psychologist.
Social Communication
Autistic people have difficulties with interpreting both verbal and non-verbal language like gestures or tone of voice. Many have a very literal understanding of language, and think people always mean exactly what they say. They may find it difficult to use or understand:
Some may not speak, or have fairly limited speech. They will often understand more of what other people say to them than they are able to express, yet may struggle with vagueness or abstract concepts. Some autistic people benefit from using, or prefer to use, alternative means of communication, such as sign language or visual symbols. Some are able to communicate very effectively without speech.
Others have good language skills, but they may still find it hard to understand the expectations of others within conversations, perhaps repeating what the other person has just said (this is called melancholia) or talking at length about their own interests.
It often helps to speak in a clear, consistent way and to give autistic people time to process what has been said to them.

Autistic people often have difficulty ‘reading’ other people – recognising or understanding others’ feelings and intentions – and expressing their own emotions. This can make it very hard for them to navigate the social world.
Autistic people may find it hard to form friendships. Some may want to interact with other people and make friends, but may be unsure how to go about it.

Repetitive behaviour and routines
The world can seem a very unpredictable and confusing place to autistic people, who often prefer to have a daily routine so that they know what is going to happen every day. They may want to always travel the same way to and from school or work, or eat exactly the same food for breakfast.
The use of rules can also be important. It may be difficult for an autistic person to take a different approach to something once they have been taught the ‘right’ way to do it. People on the autism spectrum may not be comfortable with the idea of change, but may be able to cope better if they can prepare for changes in advance.

Sensory Sensitivity

Headstart Therapies
Therapeutic support is woven into every aspect of school life, ensuring consistent and holistic care.
At Headstart School, therapeutic support is not a separate service—it is fully embedded into the daily life and learning of every pupil. Our Integrated Therapies model ensures that each child receives consistent, personalised, and holistic support across educational, emotional, and behavioural domains.
A Holistic, Embedded Approach
Therapeutic input is woven into classroom practice, outdoor learning, and residential care. Teachers, support staff, and therapists work side-by-side to ensure that strategies are consistent, responsive, and tailored to each pupil’s needs. This collaborative model allows pupils to receive support in real time, in familiar environments, and from trusted adults.
Multidisciplinary Team
Our integrated team includes:
Therapeutic Tools and Approaches
Sensory integration activities are embedded into routines to support regulation and engagement.
Communication systems such as PECS, Makaton, and visual supports are used consistently across settings.
Social and emotional learning is supported through structured programmes like SULP.
Behaviour support is guided by PBS and PRICE, ensuring a respectful, person-centred approach.
Personalised and Proactive

Land Based Learning
Practical, hands-on learning in nature that builds skills, confidence, and independence.
Land-Based and Horticulture Learning at Headstart School
At Headstart School, our land-based and horticulture provision is a core part of our therapeutic and vocational curriculum. Set within our two rural sites in East Sussex, pupils benefit from hands-on learning in natural environments that include working farms, animal care areas, and horticultural pods.
This provision offers pupils the opportunity to engage in meaningful, practical activities such as:
Animal care – including feeding, grooming, and maintaining enclosures for a variety of animals.
Gardening and horticulture – planting, growing, and harvesting fruits, vegetables, and flowers.
Environmental stewardship – learning about sustainability, composting, and caring for the land.
These experiences are designed to build confidence, responsibility, and a sense of achievement. They also support the development of key life and employability skills, such as teamwork, communication, and routine-following.
The land-based curriculum is tailored to individual needs and interests, and is often integrated with other areas of learning, including science, literacy, and personal development. For many of our pupils, this outdoor, sensory-rich environment provides a calming and motivating alternative to the traditional classroom.
Through this unique provision, Headstart School empowers pupils to develop practical skills, and grow in independence and self-esteem.

Teaching and Learning
Inspiring growth through connection, curiosity, and care.
At Headstart, we believe that great teaching is about more than just delivering content, it is about connection, curiosity, and care. Every day, our classrooms are filled with teachers who are passionate about helping young people grow, and pupils who are encouraged to think deeply, ask questions, and believe in themselves.
Our Approach to Teaching
We use Rosenshine’s Principles of Instruction as a guiding framework, not as a rigid checklist, but as a set of thoughtful, research-based habits that help us do what we do best: teach well. Each term, we focus on one of these principles as a whole school, exploring how it can make learning clearer, more engaging, and more effective. We often say, “Great teachers do more of these things,” because we know that small, consistent actions like checking for understanding or giving time to practice can make a big difference.
Champions of Teaching & Learning
Supporting this work are our Teaching and Learning Champions, experienced, trusted colleagues who bring wisdom, warmth, and a listening ear. They are not just experts; they are encouragers. Whether it is trying out a new idea, reflecting on a lesson, or just having a chat about what is working, our champions are there to walk alongside staff, helping everyone grow in confidence and creativity.
Learning Walks
We also carry out learning walks throughout the year, not to judge, but to learn. These informal visits give us a window into the wonderful things happening across the school and help us stay connected to our shared vision. They also help us shape CPD that is grounded in real classroom experiences.

A Shared Effort
At the heart of everything we do is our commitment to inclusion. For pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), we make sure their individual targets are not just known but truly understood. Teachers work closely with support staff and families to weave these goals into Headstart time and everyday lessons, so that each child feels seen, supported, and celebrated for who they are.
Teaching and learning at Headstart is a team effort. It is built on trust, shared purpose, and a belief that every child and every adult can keep learning, growing, and achieving more than they thought possible.
